one_liner: Spotify's Python audio-effects and audio-file library on a JUCE C++17 core; first-party claims of beating pySoX, SoxBindings and librosa.load.
what_it_does: A Python extension module that applies chains of audio effects to NumPy arrays: Pedalboard([Compressor(), Chorus(), Reverb()]) is a callable list of plugins, run as board(audio, sample_rate, reset=...). Built-ins include compressor, limiter, gain, chorus, phaser, distortion, filters, convolution, delay, reverb, pitch shift, resampling, bitcrush and MP3/GSM degradation. VST3 and Audio Unit plugins can be hosted with load_plugin(). pedalboard.io.AudioFile streams WAV/AIFF/FLAC/MP3/OGG (plus platform codecs) in chunks, with resampled_to() for on-the-fly resampling and AudioFile.encode() for in-memory encoding. AudioStream handles live I/O. The API differs from both pySoX's Transformer and librosa.load, so it is not a drop-in replacement for either.
how_it_is_fast: The work runs in compiled C++ inside one process. pySoX instead launches the SoX program per transform, and most of the 300x figure is that overhead. process.h copies the array once into a juce::AudioBuffer<float>. It then runs every plugin in place over 8192-sample blocks (DEFAULT_BUFFER_SIZE) with the GIL released (py::gil_scoped_release), so several Python threads can use separate cores. The DSP is JUCE's dsp module (for example juce::dsp::Reverb, a Freeverb-style design) plus Rubber Band for pitch and time stretching. Rubber Band's FFTs use vendored FFTW with AVX codelets on Linux and vDSP on macOS. The extension builds as a CMake Release with -O3 and interprocedural optimisation, and Linux x86 wheels target -mavx. File reads decode through JUCE readers, including a patched MP3 decoder, straight into the output buffer with the GIL released.
when_to_use: ML data augmentation in Python (tf.data, PyTorch DataLoader threads) that applies built-in effects to many clips. The GIL is released during processing, so threads scale across cores without multiprocessing, provided each thread owns its own plugin instances.
Replacing pySoX code that runs the sox command line once per transform. Most of the claimed 300x is removed subprocess and temporary-file overhead, so short clips gain the most.
Reading, transcoding or resampling large files from Python in constant memory: chunked AudioFile.read(), resampled_to() with O(1) memory, and WAV/FLAC/OGG/MP3 encoding without FFmpeg.
Batch rendering through third-party VST3 or Audio Unit plugins from a Python script on macOS, Windows or Linux.
when_not_to_use: C++ projects. The core is a pybind11 extension (pedalboard_native) with no C++ API or standalone library, so use JUCE's dsp classes or Rubber Band directly.

Closed-source or permissively licensed products. pedalboard is GPL-3.0 and statically bundles JUCE (GPLv3 or commercial), the VST3 SDK, Rubber Band and FFTW (GPLv2+), and LAME (relicensed to GPLv3 here).
Pipelines that must match SoX output. The effects are JUCE algorithms, not SoX ports, and the SoxBindings comparison ran each library's own effect at default parameters, so the outputs differ.
float64 processing. process() casts float64 input to float32 (astype) and always returns float32.

x86-64 CPUs without AVX. Linux x86-64 wheels require AVX, and Linux wheels up to 0.9.21 were built with -march=native and could crash with SIGILL on import on older CPUs (issue #454, fixed by PR #511 in September 2026).

integration.form: module (Python C++ extension, platform wheels on PyPI; vendored C/C++ dependencies compiled in statically)
integration.dependencies: numpy at runtime. Bundled and statically linked: JUCE 6, VST3 SDK, Rubber Band, FFTW 3 (Linux only), LAME/mpglib, libgsm, dr_wav, pybind11. A Linux source build also needs freetype and ALSA development packages.
integration.min_toolchain: Python 3.10+ (requires-python >=3.10; tested 3.10-3.15). Building from source needs C++17, CMake 3.18+, scikit-build-core >=0.5 and pybind11 >=2.9.
integration.platforms: Linux x86-64 (AVX required) and aarch64 (manylinux and musllinux wheels); macOS x86-64, arm64 and universal2; Windows amd64
integration.thread_safety: The GIL is released while plugins process and while files are read. Each Plugin holds a std::mutex, and process() locks every plugin in a chain in pointer order, so threads sharing one plugin instance run one at a time. Using the same instance twice in one chain raises an error. Concurrent reads from one AudioFile object raise 'Another thread is currently reading from this AudioFile'.

gotchas: A Pedalboard or plugin shared across threads serializes on its mutex. Build one chain per worker. The iCorv notebook's 'Pedalboard Chain' row shared one board across tf.data AUTOTUNE workers, and it is the only row where pedalboard lost to SoxBindings (357.2 s vs 305.2 s).

reset=True is the default, so each call clears delay lines and reverb tails. Chunked or streaming processing needs reset=False (README quick start). Plugins with latency get compensated output that is padded and then trimmed.

Every call copies the input array into a JUCE buffer and copies the result back, and float64 input costs an extra conversion. For very short clips the copies and Python call overhead are a large share of the time.
MP3 frames and duration are estimates until the file has been read through (exact_duration_known is False), so the length can change during reading.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: No catalogued sibling offers a Python effect chain or plugin host, so pick pedalboard for effects and for file I/O and encoding from Python. audioFlux is the catalogued choice for spectral feature extraction against librosa. libsoxr or r8brain-free-src are the C/C++ choices when the job is resampling throughput and quality rather than effects.
verified_claims_summary: The README's 300x (vs pySoX) and 4x (vs librosa.load) figures have no published method, corpus or machine; PR #85 first claimed up to 20x versus librosa.load 'without resampling', and a later commit 'tempered' the claim. The only public numbers are a third-party notebook (iCorv/pedalboard_with_tfdata: Python 3.8.11, pedalboard version and hardware not recorded) on LJ Speech at 22.05 kHz with six default-parameter effects. There SoxBindings took 38.1-130.8 s and pedalboard 10.8-32.2 s (2.4-6.3x, derived from page data). However, pedalboard ran with tf.data num_parallel_calls=AUTOTUNE while SoxBindings ran serially (the notebook says soxbindings does not allow multi-threading). No single-thread, like-for-like measurement exists behind the README's 'even when only using one thread' wording.
status_note: Actively maintained by Spotify: v0.9.25 released 2026-09-09, last commit 2026-09-23, 6.3k stars, 85 open issues and 58 open PRs. It is easy for Python users (pip wheels), but GPL-3.0 and not reusable as a C++ library.
